The roughneck grunt, Haemulopsis corvinaeformis, is a demersal fish species common along the Atlantic coast of Central and South America, where it inhabits soft-bottom habitats. Field surveys indicate that this species attains a maximum recorded total length of 29.3 centimeters [Li = 29.3 centimeters], a value consistent with its position as a medium-sized member of the Haemulidae family. Growth trajectories derived from otolith increment analysis suggest that individuals approach this asymptotic size after several years of steady somatic expansion, with the most rapid increases in length occurring during the early juvenile phase following settlement. The species is characterized by a robust, moderately compressed body form that is well-suited to benthic foraging on crustaceans and polychaetes. Comparative data from closely related congeners indicate that the ultimate length achieved by roughneck grunt is broadly similar to that reported for other demersal haemulids of comparable ecological habit, though slightly below the maximum sizes documented for larger-bodied species within the genus. This size ceiling likely reflects a combination of life-history trade-offs, including the energetic demands of reproduction and the constraints imposed by predation pressure within its shallow-water nursery and adult habitats.

In comparison to other haemulids that mature at larger sizes, the relatively modest length at puberty observed in this species may facilitate a shorter generation time, potentially conferring resilience under moderate fishing pressure. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, derived from the same allometric relationship, underscores the species' capacity to initiate reproductive output at a body mass that is only a fraction of its ultimate adult size.

The available data suggest that during peak spawning periods, females can achieve a daily reproductive output equivalent to approximately 73.6 gametes per day [Ri = approximately 73.6 gametes per day], a rate that reflects the energetic capacity for continuous batch spawning over an extended breeding season. This elevated fecundity is consistent with the species' position as a broadcast spawner that releases pelagic eggs into the water column, where high mortality during the early life stages necessitates substantial numerical investment. The daily production of gametes at this level requires significant energetic allocation toward ovarian recrudescence and may be sustained only during periods of optimal prey availability and favorable hydrographic conditions. The chorionated embryo undergoes cleavage and gastrulation in the water column, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves until the onset of exogenous feeding at mouth opening. The transition from yolk-sac larva to first feeding marks a critical bottleneck, as the tiny larvae must successfully capture suitable planktonic prey to sustain growth. The estimated egg diameter of approximately 0.85 millimeters, from which the neonatal weight is calculated, places the species within the typical size range for tropical marine fishes that produce relatively small, pelagic eggs. This lifespan, which is equivalent to roughly 5475 days, is moderately long for a fish of this body size and reproductive strategy, suggesting a life history that incorporates delayed senescence and sustained reproductive output over many breeding seasons. This asymptotic mass is consistent with the energy budget of a medium-sized demersal predator that allocates substantial resources to both somatic maintenance and annual gamete production. The comparatively extended lifespan, coupled with a moderate growth rate and iteroparous reproduction, positions the roughneck grunt as a relatively K-selected species within the haemulid family, though its early maturation and high fecundity also reflect adaptive responses to the variability of tropical coastal ecosystems.
